hints.title: Use the fixed point to reduce the algebra
hints.body: For a line with a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>-intercept <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>, write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> and impose the condition that it passes through <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
hints.recap: The fixed point relates the gradient to the intercept.
hints.pitfall: An intercept is a coordinate on an axis, not the gradient.
hints.pause: Express the gradient using c, then find the x-intercept.

recall.reminder: For an implication, begin by assuming its stated hypothesis.

hints.title: Test the two directions separately
hints.body: For P, investigate the sign of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-intercept when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. For the converse, assume a positive <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-intercept and explore which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>-intercepts can occur.
hints.recap: To refute an implication, its hypothesis must be true and its conclusion false in the same example.
hints.pitfall: A line that fails the hypothesis does not refute that implication.
hints.pause: Prove or refute each direction using the line formula or an accurate sketch.

recall.reminder: A counterexample must satisfy every condition imposed on the object.

hints.title: Translate the contrapositive precisely
hints.body: Write P as “if A, then B”. Its contrapositive is “if not B, then not A”. Use the logical relationship between these forms after you have decided P.
hints.recap: The converse reverses an implication; the contrapositive reverses and negates both parts.
hints.pitfall: The negation of positive is nonpositive, and the negation of negative is nonnegative.
hints.pause: Complete your sign argument and decide which of I, II and III must hold.

recall.reminder: An implication and its contrapositive are equivalent; its converse requires a separate check.

solution:
If the y-intercept is c<0, the line is y=(2−c)x+c. Its x-intercept is −c/(2−c)>0, because numerator and denominator are positive. Thus P is true.

The converse is false: y=−x+3 passes through (1,2) and has positive x-intercept 3, but its y-intercept is also positive.

The contrapositive is equivalent to P, so it is true. Statements I and III hold. Answer: F.
knowledgePattern: Use intercept geometry to test an implication and its reversal
